analysis.one_liner: Creates universal government-guaranteed health coverage for every legal resident, funded by new payroll and income taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for a vote: introduced in the Senate's final weeks with zero cosponsors, it died in the Finance Committee when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made every legal resident of the United States eligible for a comprehensive package of health benefits — doctor care, prescription drugs, mental health, preventive care, long-term care, and a cap on catastrophic costs — through a MediCORE card issued by their state. A new federal board would set the benefit package and approve state-run programs, with the federal government paying roughly two-thirds of the cost from a dedicated trust fund. To pay for it, the bill would impose a 2% payroll tax on employees and a 4% tax on employers (with no cap on high salaries), an income-tax surcharge of up to 6%, and would end the tax breaks that make employer-provided insurance free of income tax. It would also fold Medicare, Medicaid, and CHAMPUS into the new program.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans without insurance or with thin coverage would gain comprehensive benefits with no exclusions for pre-existing conditions, capped cost-sharing, and a limit on out-of-pocket catastrophic costs. People with employer coverage would keep comparable benefits but would no longer depend on keeping a job to stay insured. Low-income households would pay little or none of the new income surcharge, and the bill makes the WIC nutrition program an entitlement for all who qualify.

how_it_helps.text: Every legal resident, including lawful permanent residents, would be eligible for CORE services through automatic or default enrollment in a state program, issued a MediCORE card [S2][S3].

The required benefit package includes medically necessary services, prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse treatment, preventive care with no cost-sharing, long-term and custodial care, and a limit on what an individual owes for catastrophic care [S2][S3].
Cost sharing (premiums, copays, deductibles) is capped at 15% of program cost and cannot be applied to preventive services [S3].
States may not reduce coverage: a state failing Board review can be censured, have federal payments cut by no more than 5%, or have its program placed in federal receivership [S3].
The federal government would cover roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of each state's program costs through revenue-sharing payments from a dedicated trust fund [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new 4% payroll tax on all wages with no cap, lose the business deduction for health costs, and could no longer contribute to tax-free health plans. Employees would pay a new 2% payroll tax plus an income surcharge reaching 6% on adjusted gross income. Everyone with employer-sponsored insurance would lose the tax-free treatment of those benefits. Self-employed people would owe the combined 6% on their earnings.

drawbacks.text: The bill layers major new taxes on top of existing ones: a 2% employee and 4% employer payroll tax (with the employer portion entirely uncapped), plus an income surtax of up to 6% [S3].
Workers with employer coverage would lose the tax exclusion that currently shields employer health benefits from income tax, effectively a pay cut even for people who already had insurance [S3].

A nine-member federal board appointed by the President would define the benefit package, approve or reject state programs, and could place a state's health program in receivership — a large transfer of control over one-sixth of the economy to a new federal body [S2][S3].

Providers accepting program payments must accept the state-recognized payment as payment in full and cannot bill patients beyond permitted cost-sharing, which would force hospitals and doctors to absorb or renegotiate their rates [S3].

The bill repeals Medicaid, CHAMPUS, and the Health Care Financing Administration's role and supersedes ERISA, meaning a complete restructuring of every existing public and employer-based health program with a short transition timeline [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would trade a large new tax burden — falling hardest on employers and higher earners, though every worker pays the 2% employee tax — for universal coverage with real cost protections and an end to job-locked insurance. Its design is ambitious and detailed, but untested: a single federal board would set benefits for the entire country, and the transition from Medicare, Medicaid, and employer plans is abrupt. For the uninsured and for families bankrupted by medical bills (the bill's own findings cite health costs driving half of personal bankruptcies), the gains are substantial; for people satisfied with their employer coverage, the change would have been disruptive and taxing [S3].

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate's closing weeks and referred to the Finance Committee, it sat there with no cosponsors and no hearings or vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Jeffords, a Vermont Republican, introduced the MediCORE Health Act on October 5, 1992, near the end of the 102nd Congress [S1][S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and the health insurance industry, who would have faced new taxes and the loss of the employer-based insurance market, were spared; the uninsured gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and the only sponsor it ever had.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A lone Republican sponsored it and not a single senator of either party cosponsored it, and since no vote ever occurred there is no record of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would end the employer-based private insurance market: employer contributions to health plans lose their tax exclusion, and private insurance could be sold only for services not covered by MediCORE. Insurers could survive only as state-contracted claims administrators or supplemental insurers.

Employers would owe a 4% payroll tax with no wage cap and would lose health-cost deductions, though they would stop paying premiums for employee coverage. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the workers and uninsured it would have covered.
The employer-portion MediCORE tax has no income cap, and an income surtax rises to 6% of adjusted gross income; previously untaxed employer health benefits would become taxable income.
Providers get guaranteed payment for every patient, ending uncompensated care, but must accept state-set payment as payment in full with no balance billing, which would press down on rates.

industries.industry: Managed care and claims administration firms
industries.note: States may contract with private carriers and managed care organizations to run their programs, and are encouraged to offer competing delivery plans — making these firms the administrative backbone of the new public system.
